title: What you can learn from how Spotify keeps customers from cancelling
hook: Spotify runs a simple system on three things about every customer. It is fifty years old. Almost no business near 100k uses it.
caption:
What you can learn from Spotify. How they stop you from leaving, and what other businesses can copy.

Spotify runs a simple system on three things about every user. How recently they listened. How often they come back. How much they pay or cost the business to serve.

That is the whole engine.

It is not new. It is over fifty years old. I have seen very few businesses near 100k use it, even though it costs nothing to set up and explains most of what retention does and does not move.

Here is why it matters.

Your customers are not all worth the same. Some buy every week. Some buy twice a year. Two customers can look active on a chart and pull your business in opposite directions. You do not know which is which until you rank them by those three things.

How to use it in your business.

1. Pull the list of customers from the last ninety days.
2. For each one, note three things. How recently they bought. How often. How much. A rough estimate is fine.
3. Look at the top ten percent. That slice is where most of the money sits.

Treat that top slice like a real person, not a line item. Write a different email. Offer a different plan. Notice when they stop buying, on the day, not the month after.

Spotify spends a fortune on data science. They did not invent this. They used what was already there.

title: The retention problem every business faces near 100k
hook: At 100k, the revenue line looks fine. The problem is never how many leave. It is who stays.
caption:
# The retention problem for businesses near 100k

## What the chart does not tell you

At 100k, the revenue line looks fine. Each month is a little bigger than the last. Refunds stay below ten percent. Churn hovers in the single digits. If you close the laptop and look at the room, nothing feels like it is on fire.

Compound a small monthly loss over eighteen months, and you have quietly replaced more than half of your customer base. The top-line growth hides it because new customers are coming in a little faster than old ones are leaving. The day that gap narrows, which it always does, the picture changes in an afternoon.

## The real question is not how many leave, it is who stays

Two customers sign up the same week. One pays once and disappears. One pays, comes back, buys again, brings a teammate. Same product. Same price. Different kind of buyer.

The business at 100k that stalls is the one filling up with the first kind. The business at 100k that breaks through is the one slowly tilting the list toward the second.

You will not tell them apart on day one. You will tell them apart on day ninety. That is the day the business you actually have becomes visible.

## Why most teams look in the wrong place

When customers leave, most teams rewrite onboarding. They add a product tour. They test subject lines. They hire a growth engineer.

None of this changes the kind of customer coming through the door. The leverage is earlier, in the sentence on the landing page, in the promise on the ad, in what the business says it is for.

A vague promise pulls vague customers. A sharp promise pulls sharp customers. The copy is doing the sorting whether you want it to or not.

## What to look at this week

Pull your last ninety days of customers. Count how many are still with you today. Count how many pay more now than when they started. Count how many brought someone new in.

Those three counts are your business. Not the monthly revenue chart. Not the customer count. Those three.

If the counts are low, the fix is not further downstream. It is further upstream.

## Three moves that work for any business near 100k

**One. Rewrite the first sentence on your landing page.**

Read it cold. Would a stranger know, in one line, who it is for and what it solves? If not, rewrite that line before anything else. Every other channel feeds off it.

**Two. Pay closer attention to the customers you already have.**

Sort your list by who paid the most, most recently. The top ten percent is where most of the money lives. A short call, a direct message, an annual plan that saves them real money, a small add-on that fits their habit. These are where retention gets built, one customer at a time.

**Three. Fill the first two weeks after a sale.**

Most businesses near 100k leave that window empty. One welcome email, then silence. A customer who just paid is the most open to hearing from you they will ever be. A real sequence in those two weeks carries the next three months.

## What happens if you do nothing

The revenue line keeps climbing for a while. The gap between signups and losses narrows, quarter by quarter. One month the gap closes. The line flattens. The team does not know why.

That is the retention problem for businesses near 100k. It is slow and then it is fast, and it is almost always diagnosed after it has already cost a year.

## What to do if you are here now

Pull the three counts this week. Look at them honestly. Rewrite the landing page line. Fill the two-week window. Start with the top ten percent of customers and work down.

title: How Spotify knows you are about to cancel. And how to copy it.
hook: Spotify knows when you are about to cancel a month before you do. They do it with three numbers every business already has.
tweets:
Spotify knows when you are about to cancel a month before you do.

They do it with three things every business already has about its customers. Nothing clever. No new tech.

Here is the system, and how to copy it this week.

The three things are how recently the customer bought, how often they come back, and how much they pay or cost to serve.

That is the whole engine. Fifty years old. Used by banks, supermarkets, and now Spotify. Almost no business near 100k uses it.

One. How recently they bought.

A customer who bought last week is worth more than the one who bought six months ago. Not always by a little. By a lot. Sort your list by last purchase and you see the business you actually have.

Two. How often they come back.

A customer who buys twice a month is a different animal from one who buys twice a year. Same money in the till, very different future. One is a habit, the other is a memory.

Three. How much they pay or cost to serve.

A small slice of customers pays most of the bills. Another small slice pays the least and takes the most support. Do not treat those two slices the same. It will always lose you money.

Put it together. Score each customer on the three. Rank them high, middle, low.

You will find most businesses near 100k look the same. Top ten percent funds half of everything. Bottom twenty percent costs almost as much as it brings in.

What to do with the top slice.

Talk to them. A short survey. A direct line. A plan that locks them in for a year with a real saving. Let them see a face, not an autoresponder.

What to do with the bottom slice.

Accept it. Trying to save every customer costs more than it returns. Freeing up that time for the top slice pays twice.

Weekend exercise.

Pull the last ninety days of customers. Score the three. Look at the top ten percent. Write down one thing they have in common that the rest do not.

Reply with what you find. I will help you pick the first move.

hook: The only question worth asking for every new lead from now on. What would bring this person back on their own, without me chasing them?
caption:
The only question worth asking for every new lead from now on.

If your business is near 100k, start asking this every time a lead comes in.

What would bring this person back on their own, without me chasing them?

If the answer is a generic email, you are working against the grain. If the answer is a small win they got on day one, a second problem your product solves, or a friend they can share it with, the answer gets more specific the longer you sit with it.

Sit with it. The answer shows you what the rest of the funnel is missing.

title: 3 ways to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio
hook: Three ways to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio. You cannot get clients without one. You cannot build one without clients.
caption:
Three ways to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio.

You cannot get clients without a portfolio. You cannot build a portfolio without clients. Every creative strategist trying to make this move has felt it.

Here are three roads out, ranked from the fastest to the slowest.

One. A public teardown.

Pick one ad running right now. Break it down in a post. What the angle is. Why the hook works. What you would test next. One a week for eight weeks. At the end of two months, you have eight public pieces of thinking the whole market can see. That is a portfolio.

Two. A strategy document.

Pick five businesses you would like to work with. Write a one-page document for each. What you see in their ads. What you would do different. Send it, unasked. Some will ignore you. Some will not. You are doing the job to prove you can do the job.

Three. Spec work.

Pick three brands. Write the creative strategy you wish they had. Publish it with your name on it. This is the slowest of the three, but the most polished at the end.

Pick one. Ship it inside two weeks. The reason most creative strategists stay stuck in the portfolio loop is not lack of skill. It is two months of polishing a single thing that never goes out.

title: Portfolio Paradox (FB Page)
hook: Three ways to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio. The portfolio does not matter the way people think it does.
caption:
Three ways to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio.

You cannot get clients without a portfolio. You cannot build a portfolio without clients. Every creative strategist trying to make this move has felt it.

Here is the thing almost nobody says out loud. The portfolio does not matter the way people think it does.

A prospect cannot really evaluate past work. They do not know what the brief was. They do not know if the win was the writer's, the strategist's, or the media buyer's. They do not know which ad of the twelve in that folder was the one that actually worked.

What the prospect can evaluate is how you think about their business.

That is the one thing inside your control. And you can demonstrate it inside two weeks.

One. A public teardown.

Pick one ad running right now. Break it down in a post. What the angle is. Why the hook works. What you would test next. One a week for eight weeks. At the end of two months, you have eight public pieces of thinking the whole market can read. That is a portfolio.

Two. A strategy document.

Pick five businesses you would like to work with. Write a one-page document for each. What you see in their ads. What you would do different. Send it, unasked. No rate. No services page. Just the brief.

Three. Spec work.

title: The portfolio dilemma every creative strategist runs into
hook: The lie we tell ourselves. I just need to get my portfolio ready first. The truth. We are avoiding putting our thinking out in public.
caption:
The lie we tell ourselves. "I just need to get my portfolio ready first."

The truth. We are avoiding putting our thinking out in public.

Three reasons the portfolio is nice to have, not required.

1. Prospects who have hired before cannot really judge your past samples. They do not know what the brief was. They cannot tell if the win was yours.
2. Prospects who have never hired before cannot judge samples at all. They have no baseline.
3. Both kinds of prospects can judge one thing. How you think about their business, today, in writing.

title: 3 things to send instead of a portfolio
hook: Struggling to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio? Here are three things you can send to a prospect instead.
caption:
Struggling to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio?

Here are three things you can send to a prospect instead. Each takes about ninety minutes.

1. An ad teardown. Screenshot one of their current ads. Three sentences on what you would test next and why.
2. A one-page strategy document. Who the offer is for. Why it is selling now. What you would push harder on.
3. A rewrite of one of their offers with a clear hypothesis attached. Why you think this version will move the number.

Send one inside a week. The creative strategists who get hired are the ones who send the thinking first.
